en.commentary:
Three days ago Google put passive blood pressure trend tracking into the Pixel Watch 5, and last year the FDA cleared the Hilo Band as the first cuffless blood pressure device you can buy without a prescription. Both events push the same idea, that your wrist can tell you something about your blood pressure. My verdict for 2026 is that the cuff on your upper arm still decides the number your doctor will act on, and everything on your wrist is an early warning system pointing you back to that cuff.

So I rank on one thing above all others: does the device appear on the US Blood Pressure Validated Device Listing that the AHA and AMA maintain at validatebp.org. Out of hundreds of monitors sold in the US, 57 have passed the clinical accuracy protocol. That single yes-or-no fact settles more of this category than any feature comparison, and it takes thirty seconds to check before you buy.

The Omron Platinum BP5450 takes first place because TruRead automates the protocol the guidelines actually specify. Three readings, spaced, averaged, one number. Every monitor here can produce a reading. This one produces the reading your physician was taught to trust, and it does it without asking you to remember the procedure at seven in the morning.

The second thing I score hard is cuff circumference, because it is the single largest source of error in home measurement. A cuff that is too small on a large arm inflates the systolic number, and the reader never knows. Omron's wide-range D-ring cuff and A&D's 22 to 42 cm band cover almost every adult. If your upper arm measures past 42 cm, buy the manufacturer's large cuff before you buy anything else.

highlights.title: Check validatebp.org before you check the price
highlights.body: The AHA and AMA jointly maintain a public list of monitors that have passed an independent clinical accuracy protocol, and 57 devices are on it. This is the rare consumer category where a free, official, third-party answer exists for the question that matters most, and it is searchable by model number in under a minute. Every device I ranked in the top eight here is on that list. I treat presence on the VDL as the entry requirement and score everything else afterwards.

highlights.title: TruRead is the feature that turns a number into a measurement
highlights.body: Hypertension guidelines worldwide ask for multiple readings taken a minute or so apart and averaged, because a single inflation catches whatever your heart happened to be doing at that second. The Omron Platinum BP5450 and the Microlife BP B6 Connect both automate that sequence on one button press. That automation is worth more than Bluetooth, more than a colour screen, and more than a second user profile, because it removes the step people skip.

highlights.title: Cuff size is the accuracy setting nobody adjusts
highlights.body: Blood pressure is measured by occluding the brachial artery, so the fit of the band around your bicep is part of the physics. A cuff sized below your arm circumference has to squeeze harder to reach occlusion, and that extra pressure shows up as a higher systolic reading every single time. Measure your upper arm with a tape before you order. The Omron wide-range D-ring cuff spans 9 to 17 inches and the A&D band covers 22 to 42 cm, and both brands sell larger cuffs separately for arms beyond that.

highlights.title: Wi-Fi earns its keep when the person measuring lives somewhere else
highlights.body: The Withings BPM Connect is the one monitor here that uploads on its own, with no phone in the room and no app to open. For a parent measuring twice a day in another city, that difference decides whether you ever see the data. Six months of battery per charge means nobody has to remember a cable either. I rank it second overall on the strength of that one design decision.

highlights.title: Cuffless devices belong in your routine as a screening layer
highlights.body: The Hilo Band reads pulse wave shape optically from the wrist and builds a continuous 24-hour profile, which reveals overnight patterns a twice-daily cuff will never see. Google's Blood Pressure Trends on the Pixel Watch 5 works on the same physical principle and delivers one contextual insight per month. Use both as prompts to sit down and take a proper cuff reading, and take any flagged trend to your physician with cuff numbers in hand.

zh-tw.commentary:
三天前 Google 在 Pixel Watch 5 上放進被動血壓趨勢追蹤，去年 FDA 也核准了 Hilo Band 這個史上第一個免處方就能買的無壓脈帶血壓裝置。兩件事指向同一個方向，就是手腕開始能告訴你一些血壓的訊息。

我的判斷很直接。2026 年決定你醫師會不會調藥的那個數字，還是上臂壓脈帶量出來的。手腕上的東西是預警系統，它的價值在於提醒你回去乖乖用壓脈帶量一次。

所以我這份排行榜壓倒性看重一件事，就是這台機器有沒有出現在美國心臟協會與美國醫學會共同維護的驗證裝置清單 validatebp.org 上。全美國賣的血壓計數以百計，通過臨床準確度驗證的只有 57 款。這個是或否的答案，比任何規格比較都更能決定你該買哪一台，而且買之前查一下只要三十秒。

Omron Platinum BP5450 拿第一，理由是 TruRead 把指引要求的量測流程自動化了。連量三次、中間有間隔、算平均、給你一個數字。老實說，這裡每一台都量得出血壓，但只有它給的是醫師受訓時被教導要相信的那種數字，而且早上七點半睡眼惺忪的時候，你不用記得任何步驟。

第二個我打分很重的是壓脈帶臂圍，因為這是居家量測最大的誤差來源。臂圍偏粗的人用太小的壓脈帶，收縮壓會被系統性高估，而使用者完全不會察覺。Omron 的寬幅 D 環帶跟 A&D 的 22 到 42 公分帶涵蓋絕大多數成人。如果你的上臂圍超過 42 公分，先去買原廠加大壓脈帶，這件事比你選哪個品牌重要得多。

highlights.body: 美國心臟協會跟美國醫學會共同維護一份公開清單，收錄通過獨立臨床準確度驗證的血壓計，目前是 57 款。老實講，消費性商品裡很少有這種好事，你最在意的那個問題居然有免費、官方、第三方給的標準答案，而且用型號搜尋一分鐘內查得到。這份榜單前八名全部都在清單上。我把進入清單當成入場券，其他條件通通排在後面比。

highlights.title: 壓脈帶尺寸，是那個沒人去調的準確度開關
highlights.body: 血壓的原理是把上臂動脈壓到阻斷再慢慢放氣，所以壓脈帶跟你手臂的貼合程度本身就是物理的一部分。臂帶對你的臂圍來說偏小，機器就得加更大的壓力才壓得住血流，這股多出來的壓力每一次都會直接變成偏高的收縮壓。買之前先拿皮尺量一下上臂。Omron 的寬幅 D 環帶涵蓋 9 到 17 吋，A&D 是 22 到 42 公分，超過這個範圍的話兩家都有單賣加大帶。

The Omron Platinum BP5450 stays at number one and my reasoning is the same every week because the underlying facts do not move. This category is about clinical validation and cuff fit, and everything else is convenience. Omron's top model carries validation, stores readings for two users, and takes three consecutive measurements automatically and averages them, which is what actually removes the single reading noise that leads people to worry about numbers that mean nothing.

Withings BPM Connect holds second and earns it on the data path. Readings sync cleanly and the export is straightforward enough to email a physician a real record rather than a photograph of a screen. If you are managing a condition with a doctor, that continuity is worth more than a small accuracy difference.

The advice that matters most has nothing to do with which model you pick. Measure the circumference of your upper arm and buy the cuff size that fits it. A cuff that is too small reads high, sometimes by a clinically significant margin, and the standard cuff shipped in the box does not fit everyone. Manufacturers sell large and extra large cuffs separately.

Sit for five minutes, feet flat, arm supported at heart level, and take readings at the same time each day. Consistency in method matters more than the device.

A blood pressure monitor that has not been clinically validated against a reference standard produces numbers, and numbers that might be wrong are worse than no numbers because they inform decisions about medication and lifestyle.
